question: Design a planar two-layer antireflection coating on a semi-infinite glass substrate (constant refractive index 1.52, lossless), with air incidence (index 1.0). Use only lossless constant-index SiO2 (n=1.46) and TiO2 (n=2.40), one layer of each in either order. Each layer thickness must be between 40 and 160 nm. At normal incidence with s polarization, minimize the arithmetic mean power reflectance sampled from 450 to 700 nm at 5 nm spacing. A mean reflectance below 0.03 is the stated target. Use deterministic TMM only, with no RCWA, FDFD, learned surrogate or hardware. Allow at most two executed research rounds with one route and at most 64 solver evaluations per round, seed 17. After observing the actual result, choose a justified adjustment or stop. Do not claim the target was met without the spectrum and independent numeric check.

route.title: Optimization of TiO2/SiO2/Glass High-Low Antireflection Stack
route.scientific_hypothesis: A two-layer stack with the higher-index material (TiO2, n=2.40) adjacent to the glass substrate (n=1.52) and the lower-index material (SiO2, n=1.46) facing air will provide a smoother effective index transition than the reverse order, potentially yielding a lower mean reflectance across the visible spectrum when thicknesses are optimized.
route.design_principle: Stepped refractive index matching: Air (1.0) -> Low (1.46) -> High (2.40) -> Substrate (1.52). This attempts to bridge the large index gap between air and the intermediate/high layers before reaching the substrate.
soft_objectives: Minimize arithmetic mean power reflectance (s-pol, normal incidence) from 450 nm to 700 nm
manufacturing_considerations: Layer thicknesses strictly bounded between 40 nm and 160 nm
Exactly one layer of each material
theory_basis: Transfer Matrix Method for multilayer interference
Quarter-wave transformer approximation as an initial guess heuristic
expected_advantages: The high-index layer next to the glass may reduce the reflection coefficient at the second interface compared to a direct SiO2-Glass interface.
Two degrees of freedom (thicknesses) allow tuning for broadband performance.
known_risks: The index step from SiO2 (1.46) to TiO2 (2.40) is large and may cause significant internal reflection if not perfectly tuned.
Thickness constraints (40-160 nm) may prevent reaching the theoretical global minimum if it lies outside this box.
Two layers may be insufficient to achieve the <0.03 target over such a wide bandwidth.

Optimize the thickness of Layer 1 and Layer 2 to minimize the arithmetic mean power reflectance for s-polarized light at normal incidence over the wavelength range 450 nm to 700 nm (5 nm spacing). Constraints: Thickness of Layer 1 in [40, 160] nm; Thickness of Layer 2 in [40, 160] nm. Use seed 17 for the optimizer. Maximum 64 solver evaluations. Report the optimal thicknesses, the full reflectance spectrum, and the calculated mean reflectance. route.title: Expansion to 3-Layer SiO2/TiO2 Antireflection Stack
route.scientific_hypothesis: Adding a third layer to the two-material system (SiO2/TiO2) provides sufficient degrees of freedom to reduce the arithmetic mean reflectance over 450-700 nm below the ~0.019 level achieved by the optimal 2-layer configuration, potentially approaching the soft target of 0.03 with greater margin or exceeding it significantly.
route.design_principle: Multi-layer impedance matching: A three-layer structure allows for a smoother transition of effective refractive index from air (1.0) to glass (1.52) across the bandwidth, mitigating the sharp resonances inherent in two-layer designs. Specifically, a Low-High-Low (LHL) or High-Low-High (HLH) sequence can broaden the antireflection band.
route.proposed_topology: Air | Layer 1 | Layer 2 | Layer 3 | Glass Substrate. Total finite layers: 3. Material assignment hypothesis: Layer 1=SiO2, Layer 2=TiO2, Layer 3=SiO2 (LHL configuration).
soft_objectives: minimize arithmetic mean power reflectance (s-pol, normal incidence) over 450-700 nm
manufacturing_considerations: All layers must remain within 40-160 nm thickness bounds
Only SiO2 and TiO2 materials permitted
theory_basis: Thin-film interference theory suggests that N-layer AR coatings can achieve lower average reflectance over a broad band than (N-1)-layer coatings given the same material constraints.
Quarter-wave stack principles adapted for broadband AR: centering optical thicknesses near lambda/4 at the geometric mean of the band edges.
expected_advantages: Broader spectral low-reflectance region compared to 2-layer design.
Lower arithmetic mean reflectance due to extra tuning parameter.
Potential to push mean reflectance well below 0.01.
known_risks: Optimizer may converge to a local minimum where the third layer has negligible effect (thickness near bound or effectively zero optical impact).
Increased complexity might lead to thinner layers approaching the 40 nm lower bound, increasing sensitivity to fabrication errors (though not modeled here).
